content.thinking:
I'm avoiding the other sample files and focusing on designing a League of Legends-style treasure hoard prop group, with exaggerated dynamic shapes, saturated colors, and glowing magical details visible from a top-down camera—planning a coin mound, an open glowing chest, crown, goblets, and gems.

I'm working out the composition: a mound of individually merged coin cylinders (roughly 400 coins across a few colors) sitting on a cave-floor dais, aiming for a hand-painted, lightly cel-shaded look with gold, crimson, purple-stone, and teal tones accented by a strong hextech cyan glow on gems and magic wisps.

For the base I'm sculpting an irregular stone dais with a glowing cyan rune ring (via a decal texture) for top-down readability, then building a chest at the back-center — a box body with an arched, tilted-open lid, gold-brass straps, corner caps, lock plate, and rivets, topped with a mounded, glowing pile of coins spilling over the rim. Since the lid needs to move, I'm setting up a root joint plus a hinge joint for the lid specifically, assigning the lid's parts to that hinge bone while everything else attaches to root.

I'm working out the hinge rotation math: building the lid geometry in its closed position, then posing the hinge joint to swing it open. Since the chest faces forward (+Z) and I need the front edge of the lid to rotate upward, the rotation about the X-axis needs to be negative (around -105°) based on how the sine term maps forward-pointing coordinates during rotation.

For the chest's overall orientation, I'm deciding to keep it axis-aligned facing +Z rather than adding yaw, to simplify the geometry composition—though I consider whether a helper function could apply per-part rotation around each part's own origin if I want subtle variation later.

Now I'm sketching the overall layout: the chest sits at the back of a roughly 1.1m radius floor circle, with a coin mound spilling out in front composed of individually placed and tilted coin instances over a heap-height function, plus a crown resting on the mound's top-left.

I'm then placing a league-style crown with curved spiky points and gem tips tilted onto the mound, followed by three varying-sized goblets (one tipped over spilling coins, one silver) and scattering many faceted gems and crystal clusters in cyan, ruby, emerald, and amethyst colors throughout the scene.

I'm also adding coin stacks of varying heights at the right, draped pearl necklaces and gold torus rings, stacked gold ingots, a leather coin sack spilling at the front, and a large glowing cyan hextech crystal cluster at the back-left with small floating glowing octahedra as magical motes.

For scope, I'll keep extras modest: a stone dais base with cracked edges, a few low-poly cave rocks, and a small skull detail near the back for storytelling, while coins will be built as small merged cylinder shapes.

Writing coin texture logic...

Since UVs overlap confusingly between caps and sides, I'm considering manually overwriting the UV attribute after geometry creation, using the geometry's groups to distinguish torso versus cap faces and assign cleaner coordinates to each.

At ~270 texels per meter a coin face only gets ~16 texels across, too coarse for an emblem; bumping paint resolution to 2048 roughly doubles texel density to ~30 texels per coin, which is acceptable with a 4096 atlas. Since each part gets unique UV space in the paint sheet rather than sharing instances, cost scales with total merged coin area, which is fine — but I still need to account for normals in model space for the cel shading function.

I'm structuring coin paint as nested cel-shaded paints that resolve per point/normal, with edge detection and tone-based patterns, returning different gold/silver cel paints depending on material. I'm grouping coins by three tones (gold, rose gold, silver), each merged part assigned its own coinPaint call, and confirming merged mesh parts with bone/position offsets are supported. For the emblem itself, I'm sketching the math for a diamond shape and ring using absolute coordinate thresholds to fake a raised rim and center design without needing actual geometry.

I'm now budgeting triangle counts for the coin pile: estimating segment counts per coin (8-sided cylinders), figuring roughly 32 tris per coin, and scaling that against hundreds of coins to stay under a 60k triangle budget—deciding to use fewer segments for buried coins and reserve detail for visible ones. I'm also planning to fill the heap's visual gaps with an underlying lathe-shaped mass painted in a mottled gold cel style, so there are no visible holes beneath the surface coins, and noting the joint/bone structure stays minimal (just root and lid). Finally, I'm starting to design a gem geometry function that builds a brilliant-cut shape by combining a frustum crown and a pavilion cone from cylinder primitives.

Now I'm thinking through how to color and shade the gems—weighing flat full-bright glow versus normal lighting, and settling on a three-tone cel paint approach (highlight, lit, shadow) so facets read crisply against the faceted normals, applying this same three-tone scheme as the standard material style across the piece.

I'm also planning the material budget, favoring custom paints over flat colors since paints don't count against the limited flat-color slots, then moving to wood details for the chest using a grain-and-plank paint function that picks board color by position.

For the chest hardware, I'm designing gold metal bands with riveted spheres, brass corner caps, and a glowing cyan keyhole set into a big gold lock plate, with crimson velvet lining the inside of the lid. I want the chest silhouette stylized with a flared top, arched lid, chunky studs, and ornate gold scrollwork along the corners, then I'm working out the body geometry using a tapered frustum box shape for the main form.

Rather than fighting with ambiguous box orientation, I'll extrude a trapezoid profile along the depth axis for the body, then decide how to handle the open-top cavity cheaply: a solid body box topped with a heap of gold filling to the rim, with just enough velvet trim visible at the lip to sell the hollow look without modeling full interior walls.

For the heap itself, I'll use a flattened gold ellipsoid scaled to sit low and wide, dotted with coins, which reads as an overflowing treasure pile without needing complex geometry.

For the lid, I'm extruding a half-ellipse arch profile along the hinge axis, working out which local axes map to the extrusion thickness so the curved dome shape sits correctly over the chest body.

Now I'm building the lid as a thin curved shell rather than a solid arch -- an outer and inner arc offset by a small thickness to form a band, plus flat half-disc end caps on both sides, with velvet lining distinguished on the inner face versus the wooden outer face.

For the paint logic, I'm using the dot product between the surface normal and the radial vector from the hinge center to decide which points are outer wood versus inner velvet. Then I'm adding decorative gold bands running across the lid at a few positions by extruding a slightly offset arc outline.

Now I'm working out the hinge geometry: the joint sits at the back edge where the lid meets the chest, and I'm rotating the closed lid about this axis by -110° to get the open pose. I'm tracking how the forward-extending point of the lid maps after rotation — computing its new vertical and depth position so the opened lid correctly swings up and slightly back relative to the hinge.

The chest ends up around 0.85m tall total, with reasonable proportions for the whole prop group — coins, crown, and goblets sized slightly larger than realistic dimensions for a stylized fantasy look, similar to game-asset exaggeration.

I'm designing the dais now: a low stone ring platform (radius 1.25, height 0.07) that everything sits on top of at y=0.08, plus a glowing cyan rune ring texture laid flat on its surface using a rotated plane geometry.

For the stone texture itself, I'm using a cel-shaded flagstone pattern with crack lines drawn where cell boundaries are close together, giving it a weathered paving look, and considering adding small stone teeth around the dais edge.

I'm adding low-poly rock clusters at the back-left and back-right using scaled icosahedrons in purple-grey, with a cluster of cyan crystals growing from the back-right rocks — hexagonal prism shapes topped with pyramid points, glowing with a flat cyan-to-light-blue color scheme.

Actually, a cleaner compromise: keep most crystals with painted toon facets for readable detail, and reserve true glow for just a few accent shards or embedded gems, so I get both faceted texture and a strong glow highlight without losing the silhouette.

For the crown itself, I'm settling on a tapered lathe band with seven alternating long/short blade-like points, each tipped with a gem, plus one large glowing cyan centerpiece gem in a gold bezel at the front, with a visible red velvet interior.

Still writing crown geometry...

Setting up a local-frame helper with origin and quaternion so I can map local points and directions into world space, letting the crown's lathe axis and extrude directions follow the tilted orientation cleanly.

For the goblets, I'm designing a lathed profile with foot, knop stem, and flared cup, giving the cup actual wall thickness by painting outer and inner profiles differently based on normal direction, plus a ring of gem studs and a glowing violet or cyan potion filling the inside.

I'm also planning a tipped goblet lying on its side spilling coins and gems across the floor, plus a scattering of roughly 40 faceted gems of varying sizes built from merged cylinder and cone geometry to form a classic brilliant-cut diamond shape.

For coloring, I'll apply a toon shader with strong highlights to each gem, and decide which elements should actually glow — crystals, the rune ring, keyhole, potion, and the crown's central gem — while leaving the cyan gems non-luminous for contrast.

Now for the gold ingots, I'm shaping them as stacked trapezoid bars extruded to a thickness, with a toon gold paint and a raised embossed panel on top to fake a stamped marking rather than using a decal.

For coin stacks, I'm layering individual coin shapes vertically with slight random offsets and rotations to make them look naturally piled, and adjusting the torso UV mapping so the paint shader picks up fractional stripes for a reeded-edge coin look.

I'm now thinking through a draped gold chain with a glowing pendant, built as a catmull-rom path with beads swept along it, and I need an analytic heap height function—a sum of gaussian bumps—so coins and necklace positions sit coherently on the mound surface with proper normals for tilt. I'm also working out the dais geometry and how the heap should spill forward from the chest's front edge without clipping through it.

Still generating coin placement code...

I'm modeling the heap as several ellipsoid "lumps," each defined by its center and radii, with a height function taking the max cap height across all lumps so they blend into one pile. Coins get placed on the upper hemisphere surface of each lump's sphere, rejecting positions where another lump's surface would be higher, so only the visible outer coins get drawn.

I'm laying out six or seven overlapping lumps for the main hoard, side piles, and a dome tucked under the chest, each with its own center, radii, height, and base elevation, then sketching out roughly how many coins each lump should get.

Adding remaining lumps plus a few small stacks gets me to around 600 coins total, which at 32 triangles each lands near 19k triangles — reasonable. Then I'm figuring out the painted texel budget: coin faces take about 3.4 m², other painted surfaces like the dais top add up to roughly 15 m², and working out texel density gives something like 191 texels/m at 1024 resolution or 380 at 2048.

Going with a 2048 paint size feeding a 4096 atlas feels like the right call -- the coin's small radius still ends up with enough texels to read clearly, and the octagonal cap UVs should hold up fine too.

Now I'm thinking through the palette with a League of Legends-style saturated, bold look: lit gold around #ffc83a with a pale highlight near #fff0a0, and working out that the shadow tone shifts toward orange-red rather than violet based on the hue math. I'm pairing that with rose-gold/copper coins near #ff9a52, cool bluish silver around #cfe3ff, and considering a deep purple-brown for the chest wood, all keeping with that heavily saturated stylized aesthetic.

I'm settling on a ruddy chest wood #7a3f35 with gold bands, crimson velvet #d6204a, and hextech cyan/magenta accents against a blue-violet slate dais for strong warm-cool contrast. I'm sketching out a toon shading helper that buckets a surface's light-dot value into highlight, base, or shadow colors, with a lighten function mixing the base color toward white for the highlight tone -- and I'm reasoning that since paints sample interpolated normals per texel, the cel-shading boundaries should render smoothly across curved meshes.

I'm deciding to skip back-light shadow tones and ink outlines to stay true to the stylized look, then moving on to sizing: defining the dais lathe profile with beveled edges, considering whether to add a raised stone curb or just a painted gold inlay ring, and working out where to place a glowing rune ring so it doesn't overlap the loot heap.

Now I'm adjusting item placement so the heap lumps stay within the dais radius and don't collide with the rune ring, and working through the camera/handedness math to confirm which direction (+X) appears on which side of the screen from the viewer's perspective.

I'm placing specific objects next: the chest centered toward the back with its lid opening behind it, a crown tilted forward resting on one of the gold heap lumps, and starting to position the goblets among the hoard.

Now I'm working out where to put each goblet — one standing upright on a heap, a potion goblet with cyan glow near the dais, and a silver one tipped over with coins spilling toward the front. I'm also figuring out placement for the coin stacks near the chest's right side.

Then I'm laying out the rest of the hoard: a pyramid of ingots near the chest's left side, glowing crystal clusters flanking the back corners with scattered floating motes, a leaning sack of spilled coins at the right front with a cord-tied neck, and now considering adding a skull near the left side for extra detail.

I want a small half-buried skull with glowing cyan eyes near the front-left dais, plus a draped necklace with a ruby pendant swept using a catmull path, a few gold rings with gem tops scattered on the heap, and about sixty scattered gems and loose coins covering the dais floor.

For extra flourish I'm considering a handful of floating motes — maybe tiny spinning octahedra or glowing coins with star-sparkle textures — but keeping their height capped around 1.0m so they don't blow out the overall bounding size.

Since cards are symmetric, I'll use cross:true with size 0.12, offsetting frames slightly below center. Now tallying part counts: merged coin pieces, roughly six gems per color, around thirty crown pieces, and three goblets.

For scatter elements I want hundreds of parts total but shouldn't over-merge since the budget allows up to 1000 — I'll keep crown points individual, place crystals and hero gems as separate parts rather than merging by color, landing somewhere around 250-400 parts overall.

Setting up imports and helper utilities for the build script...

Adding more shading tiers...

Writing coin paint logic...

Switching to a hexagonal coin emblem with a center dot and face detail, then starting the coin geometry builder with a cylinder base.

Mapping out vertex counts for the cylinder's torso and caps to figure out exactly which UV coordinates to shift for the custom coin texture layout.

For the coins I'll vary scale and radius slightly across instances, and merge all the geometries using mergeGeometries with matching position/normal/uv attributes, keeping smooth shading on the sides. I'm also writing a helper function to position each coin given its location, surface normal, and tilt.

Rather than using Three.js's setFromUnitVectors directly, I'll use the aim helper to get a quaternion aligning the coin's up axis to the surface normal, then add random tilt and spin for variety. I'm organizing merged geometries by tone into batches, and building functions for coin heaps, lumps, and spillage from tipped goblets, sacks, and the floor, all feeding into a common addCoin helper that takes tone, position, and orientation.

Now I'm working out the chest's part API, deciding to explicitly bind most parts to the root bone rather than relying on nearest-joint heuristics, so lid parts only attach to the lid joint when intended. I'm sketching the chest body dimensions—width, depth, height—and planning the front profile as an extruded trapezoid with slightly flared top edges before working out the thickness axis.

For the wood texturing, I'm figuring out how to map plank patterns across different faces using local surface coordinates, drawing dark seam lines at regular intervals and varying brown tones per plank for a toon-shaded wood look.

I also want to add grain streaks using anisotropic noise stretched along the plank direction, selecting between a few precomputed toon wood color variants via a hash of the plank index. Then I'm planning gold metal straps as proud boxes wrapping vertically around the body at specific x-offsets on the front face.

Still building the strap geometry...

Beyond the straps, I want a horizontal gold band wrapping the base, rivets as merged spheres along each strap row, and gold corner brackets with small spheres at the top and bottom corners. Finally I'm sketching a front lock plate as a shield-shaped extrusion in gold with a glowing cyan keyhole detail.

For the lock itself, I'm picturing a hexagonal cyan gem using a six-sided cylinder that glows, mounted on the body with the latch hanging open since the lid is raised. I'm also adding chunky gold claw feet via short cylinders at the corners, raising the chest body slightly off the base, and finishing with gold trim boxes along the top rim plus a velvet floor panel inside.

Now I'm working out the curved lid geometry, parameterizing an arc profile with height and depth values and computing outer edge points by stepping through angles from back to front to shape the dome.

The lid's half-depth sets the hinge point at the back-bottom edge of the lid, so I'm defining a joint there that lets the lid rotate about that hinge with an aim constraint tying it to the parent root.

Now I'm building the end plates of the lid as filled half-ellipse extrusions offset along X, plus the main shell as a thicker extrusion spanning the lid's width.

For the lid's surface paint, I'm deciding wood versus velvet based on the normal direction relative to the hinge-centered radial vector in the YZ plane — outward-facing normals get wood, inward-facing get crimson velvet, while the flat end faces along X default to wood since their radial dot product is near zero.

For the iron bands on the lid, I'm planning the arc outlines to be slightly offset from the main shell curves for overlap, with a thickness around 0.08 positioned near the sides, plus a thicker center section to accommodate the lock tab.

Writing tufted velvet pattern code...

I realize constant-across-thickness patterning just gives stripes, not diamonds, so I need to bring in the x-coordinate for one axis and an arc-length angle for the other to get a proper diagonal diamond weave across the wall surface.

Now I'm shifting to designing the crystals: tall hexagonal prisms made from a shaft and tip part with leaning rotation, using two cyan glow shades to differentiate the base and point of each crystal.

For the base, I'm sketching a lumpy icosahedron rock cluster with toon violet paint, plus sparkle star SVGs with a soft glow and a rune ring SVG made of circular strokes and rotated glyph marks around the border.

I'm working through scale conversions: the 1024px texture maps to a 200-unit viewBox at roughly 5 pixels per unit, so I'm setting strokes around 1.6 units to stay visible, and translating the ring radius and dais size into real meters on a 2.5m plane to make sure the gem heap and rune ring fit without overlapping edges.

Now I'm defining the gem variety — brilliant cuts using merged cylinder/cone shapes with flat shading, octahedrons stretched vertically for diamond/kite forms, and low-detail dodecahedrons for rounder stones, each placed with some random tilt. I'm picking saturated gem colors: ruby red, sapphire blue, emerald green, amethyst purple, and a golden topaz tone.

I'm setting up toon-shaded materials for each gem with lighter highlight mixes for a glossy, high-contrast look, then writing a generic heap-sampling function that picks a lump weighted by surface area and computes a random point on it using azimuth and elevation sampling for placing gems embedded partway into the surface.

I need to reject sampled points that fall underneath other overlapping lumps or inside the chest body's bounding box, since those positions would end up hidden—checking against the height field and the chest's wall boundaries to filter out invalid coin placements.

Now I'm turning to the goblets, designing their lathe profile as a series of radius-height points tracing the foot, stem, knop, and cup from base to rim and back down the inner wall to the axis, forming a closed loop suitable for revolution with a crease angle threshold to keep edges sharp.

I'm exaggerating the scale slightly beyond realistic goblet proportions for a stylized league-trophy look, planning to add swept bezier handles with gold tubing, gemstone accents, and a decorative band around the cup. I'm now working out placement for the first gold goblet variant, checking it against the heap and ground height function to avoid overlapping other objects and embedding its base properly into the terrain.

I'm refining the base placement logic so the goblet's foot sits flush against the sloped heap rather than floating, then sketching a second silver goblet variant with a glowing potion inside. I'm reworking the overall layout coordinates for the chest, heap, crown, and both goblets to avoid collisions, deciding to drop one of the lamp positions in favor of placing the silver goblet directly on the dais beside the chest.

Now I'm positioning a third tipped goblet lying on its side at the front, with coins spilling from its rim, working out the horizontal axis orientation and foot-bottom height needed so it rests naturally against the heap.

Working out the tilt geometry...

With the foot radius smaller than the cup, the foot's bottom edge actually floats above the floor—so the tipped goblet can't rest flat on the base alone. A real tilted goblet would balance on the rim's edge and the foot's edge together, not the full foot bottom.

Actually I had the tilt backwards — to make both the foot and rim edges tangent, the thinner end needs to sit lower, so the axis should tilt the opposite direction, rising toward the rim.

Now I'm planning the potion goblet's details: a glowing liquid disc near the rim with violet/cyan highlights, plus a few tiny glowing spheres floating above to suggest rising bubbles, then moving on to the crown's position and tilt above it.

Setting up a coordinate frame helper for mapping local crown geometry into world space with a tilted axis, then defining the crown's lathe profile for the band shell with inner and outer wall thickness.

Still writing crown geometry...

Still designing spire geometry...

Still positioning spires around the crown ring, computing tangent and up vectors for each tilted frame, then applying gold toon shading with diamond engraving to the lathe shapes. Now I'm starting the skull geometry with a scaled sphere base.

Next I'm building the loot sack — a lathed burlap profile with flared cuff, stitched texture, a gold coin emblem, rope tie with tassels at the neck, and a scattering of coins spilling from the opening. Then I move to the rings with gem-topped toruses and start laying out the necklace chain path.

For the chain, I'm draping catmull-rom points over the coin heap's contours, with pearl beads strung along the curve and a separate gold chain, finishing in a ruby teardrop pendant at the lowest hang point. I'm also scattering around 40 individual coins across the dais floor at randomized polar positions, keeping them away from the heap and other objects, lying mostly flat with slight tilt variation for realism.

Now I'm building the stacked coin columns—several towers of varying heights (some leaning or toppled like dominoes), mixing gold, silver, and copper coin materials with the top coin's emblem left visible. For the gold bars, I'm constructing a staggered pyramid of trapezoidal ingots extruded along their length, arranged in layered rows near the base of the scene.

Each bar gets a toon-shaded gold material plus a small stamped crest decal (a dark hexagonal mark, no text) applied as a thin plane on one face. I'm placing six bars total, then moving on to add low-poly rock and crystal clusters toward the back of the scene.

I want the rock clusters positioned near the dais edges, shaded in a purple-slate toon palette with lighter highlights and deep shadow tones, each holding a handful of crystals -- mostly cyan for the main hextech accent, with a few smaller violet crystals mixed in for contrast. For the dais surface itself, I'm writing a cell-based flagstone pattern with toon stone coloring and inked crack lines along the seams.

I work out the lighting math so top-facing surfaces read as the base saturated tone rather than the highlight, tuning the dot-product thresholds against the key light direction until the up-normal falls into the "base" bucket correctly. I also want to add a thin gold filigree ring around the dais edge for a decorative inlay touch.

I'm also sketching out small hex-shaped stone pillars with glowing cyan gems topping them, placed at radius around the dais corners to frame the diorama like a hexgate, while making sure their angles avoid overlapping with the chest lid at the back.

Then I'm checking overall scale — settling on roughly a 2.6 m diameter dais, though considering shrinking it slightly to keep the composition tighter.

Now I'm setting up the imports and type definitions needed for the geometry builder, pulling in math, paint, path, and texture utilities along with toon shading and glow helpers, making sure I only import what's actually used to avoid lint errors.

Defining the builder structure...

I'm checking the lighting math for each face direction to confirm shading bands are correct, then starting on a wood paint function with toon-shaded rows based on surface position.

Now I'm distinguishing how plank orientation differs between extruded wall body and lid shell, and defining a seam color for low-fraction boundaries to darken plank edges.

Adding grain noise and seam detail, plus defining velvet crimson, gold metal, and stone dais paint variants before setting up the part-creation helper functions.

I need a safe geometry merge helper that throws if merging fails, and I'm being careful about indexed versus non-indexed geometries—keeping rivets, gems, and boxes indexed while isolating non-indexed shapes like icosahedron rocks and octahedron gems from any merge calls. Now I'm setting up a transform helper for positioning, rotating, and scaling geometries before starting on the crown piece.

I'm defining a frame class that computes world-space points and directions from an origin and quaternion, letting me pass either arrays or Vector3 instances interchangeably. I'm also deciding how the aim function handles orientation—aligning a local axis to a direction with an optional up vector for yaw control—and setting up how parts attach quaternions directly for things like gems, while merged geometries get transformed manually. Now I'm starting the coin geometry with its radius and thickness constants.

Writing coin UV mapping and placement logic...

Still writing height function...

Defining the lump list and positions...

Adding a sack spill near the dais and tallying up coin counts across all the lumps, stacks, and spill areas — roughly 620 coins total.

I'm figuring out the triangle budget, assigning gold/rose/silver tones randomly per coin with gold dominant, and giving heap coins varied tilt angles so they stick out naturally. Now I'm writing the gem generation logic, creating brilliant-cut gem geometries per color and placing them with position, orientation, and size.

I'm positioning gems by sinking their tip into the surface for a buried, embedded look, with slight random tilts for loose gems scattered on the dais or heap so they sit naturally rather than lying flat.

For gem shapes, I'm exploring different cuts: a stepped rectangular form using a scaled, bevel-like box, and a bipyramid shape built from two merged cones (short on top, longer below) to mimic an octahedral crystal. I want variety across gem types—brilliant cuts with eight sides, bipyramids with six, and rounder cabochon forms.

For cabochons I'll use a flattened sphere (scaled down in height) for that smooth domed look. Gems get toon shading with a brighter highlight mixed toward white and shadow tones, no ink outline. A few large cyan gems scattered on the hoard will glow flat for emphasis, plus sparkle highlights placed at roughly a dozen points.

Now I'm defining a crystal-building function that constructs a shaft from a cylinder and a pointed tip from a cone, stacking them along a direction vector with proper placement and orientation—using separate parts for shaft and tip so I can apply different glow colors to each.

I decide glowing flat materials still read fine since diffuse lighting adds on top of the emissive glow, preserving some facet shading, so I don't need extra tricks for texture. I add floating glowing motes as small bipyramids at varying heights, then start writing the actual build function, setting up the builder with the hoard's name and metadata.

Writing SVG rune ring code...

Now I'm sketching the stamp SVG with a rounded rectangle outline in dark orange and a hex emblem, checking that the stroke width scales cleanly at 256px. I'm also considering how a sparkle or glow card should pick up tint color from the card's own color string rather than staying plain white.

For the cards API, I'm figuring out that `cards()` takes frames, texture, and style options and returns an array of meshes that `glow()` can target, and that each card should inherit bones from its frame so a `bone: root` option keeps things rigid. I'm planning to import `frame` from the frame module and define a "lid" joint parented to root with a hinge position and direction, trying to settle on `dir: [1,0,0]` for the hinge axis.

I'm setting up the pose call to rotate the lid about its X axis by -108 degrees, making sure the lid-attached parts get built before the pose is applied since surface placement afterward is irrelevant. For the exterior of the lid, I'm placing a central hex gem with a gold bezel near the top of the arc, alongside bands and other ornamental details.

Now I'm adding a lock hasp -- a small gold shield-shaped tab attached to the lid's front edge, bone-parented to the lid so it swings up when the lid opens, with coordinates defining its extruded shield outline and placement near the front lower edge. I'm also starting on the body's static lock plate that pairs with it, positioned near the top front with a keyhole-glow hex gem.

Now I'm positioning the front straps as boxes flanking the chest body and reconsidering the body shape itself -- rather than a straight box, flaring the trapezoid wider at the top for a more exaggerated chest silhouette, which means I'll need to adjust the strap alignment to match the new flared outline.

Still placing corner straps...

For the body paint I'm using the extruded wood shape with a slight bevel, and for rivets I'm placing small merged gold spheres spaced along the straps, concentrated near the front chest area, then merging them into a single gold toon-painted part for efficiency.

Now I'm adding a velvet interior slab beneath the rim, a gold wooden trim frame around the chest opening sized to fit above the body top, and setting up dimensions for the lid's arc shape and shell thickness before defining the function that generates the lid's outline points.

For the end plates, I'll just extrude filled half-ellipses at the sides as simple wood pieces, skipping any gold rim detailing on them for now.

Now I'm working out the gold bands that wrap around the trunk's shell, defining outer and inner arc offsets to give them thickness, and deciding to place three bands at x positions -0.3, 0, and 0.3.

Time to actually write the code now — I'll build the full file in one pass, preview it, and iterate from there. I'm also sketching out the pillar design: a hexagonal lathed stone profile topped with a floating glowing gem (a spinning bipyramid in cyan) plus gold rings, and defining a custom toon-shaded stone material.

For the floor coin placement, I'm working out a collision-avoidance heuristic that samples positions and rejects ones too close to existing scene objects — tracking rough circles for the chest, ingots, crystals, pillars, sack, skull, goblet, and other props so new items don't overlap them.

Now I'm designing a few scattered coin stacks near the chest with varying heights and tilts, plus a standalone coin balanced on its edge and a few hero gems placed deliberately for visual focal points.

I'm also sketching a burlap sack with an open mouth, defining its silhouette for a lathe profile so coins can spill visibly from its rim.

I'll keep the sack upright without tilting, adding a gold cord tie with tassel and a front patch emblem with a coin design rendered through conditional paint logic, plus burlap weave striping based on vertical position.

For the lathe shapes, I'm tuning segment counts for a low-poly look: around 10 segments for goblets and 14 for the crown band so the 7 spires align every other segment, and I'll handle the crown's deg-based patterning within the lathe frame rather than worrying about fine paint details elsewhere.

For the heap base, I'm using slightly undersized spheres (about 0.96 scale) under the coins so there's no z-fighting and no visible gaps, with toon-shaded gold deep coloring and coins embedded at half-thickness on the sphere surface.

Now I'm sketching the sampling function for scattering coins across a lump: biasing the vertical position toward the top with a power curve so coins pile up like a mound, then deriving the horizontal radius from that height to keep points on the ellipsoid surface, and converting an azimuth angle into x/z offsets scaled by the lump's radii.

I'm computing the surface normal at each sampled point by scaling the offset from center by the inverse squared radii, then rejecting points that are covered by another lump stacked higher at that location using a height-map lookup, while allowing a point to match its own lump's height exactly. Coin tilt will be derived from this normal with a small random jitter, and the gem sampler will reuse this same lump-sampling logic but with different weighting.

Writing goblet builder function...

Now I'm computing the gem band placement around the cup's gold trim, interpolating the outer surface radius at that height to position gems evenly around the ring.
